questions.stem: Which pairing of a structural member with the main type of load it carries is correct?
options: A column holding up a building: tension
The chain holding up a chandelier: compression
A bolt joining two plates that slide past each other: tension
The main cable of a suspension bridge: tension
questions.explanation: A cable holding up a load is pulled from both ends, so it is in tension. A column is squashed, so it is in compression, and a hanging chain is in tension. A bolt resisting two plates sliding across it is in shear.

questions.stem: What do shear forces do to a body?
options: They act along the length of a member and tend to stretch it out
They act along the length of a member and tend to squash it
They act only at the centre of mass of a body and tend to make it fall over
They act parallel to a surface and tend to make layers slide past each other
questions.explanation: Shear forces act parallel to a surface, in opposite directions on either side, so one layer tends to slide over the next. Stretching along the length is tension and squashing along it is compression.

questions.stem: A horizontal beam supported at both ends sags under a load at its centre. Which parts of the beam are in tension and compression?
options: The top surface is stretched and the bottom surface is compressed
The whole depth of the beam is in tension along its length
The whole depth of the beam is in compression along its length
The top surface is compressed and the bottom surface is stretched
questions.explanation: As the beam bends into a sag, the top surface becomes shorter, so it is in compression, and the bottom surface becomes longer, so it is in tension. Somewhere between is a neutral layer that is neither stretched nor squashed.

questions.stem: Why are steel reinforcing bars placed near the bottom of a concrete beam that is supported at its ends?
options: The bottom of the beam is in tension, and steel carries the tension that concrete cannot
The bottom of the beam is in compression, and steel resists compression better than concrete
Steel is less dense than concrete, so placing it low lowers the beam’s centre of mass
Steel bars stop the concrete from expanding in hot weather, which would crack the top
questions.explanation: In a beam sagging between supports, the lower part is stretched. Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so it would crack there; steel has a high tensile strength and carries the tension. Steel is denser than concrete, not less dense.

questions.stem: The Leaning Tower of Pisa leans noticeably but does not topple. Why?
options: Its lean has moved its centre of mass down below the ground
The vertical line through its centre of mass still passes inside its base
Its foundations pull it downward with a force greater than its weight
Its centre of mass lies directly above the edge of its base
questions.explanation: A structure resting on a base stays up as long as the line of action of its weight, through the centre of mass, falls inside the base. Then the weight’s torque about the edge tends to restore it. If that line passed outside the base, the weight would tip it over.

questions.stem: Why is a low structure with a wide base more stable than a tall, narrow one?
options: Its weight acts at the edge of its base rather than at its centre of mass
A wide base always adds a lot of extra mass, so the structure can no longer be tipped
Its centre of mass sits outside its base, so gravity holds it down
Its centre of mass must be raised and moved further before it passes outside the base
questions.explanation: To topple, a structure must tilt until its centre of mass is directly over the pivot edge. A low centre of mass over a wide base must tilt much further to get there, and the weight provides a large restoring torque. Weight always acts at the centre of mass.

questions.stem: A uniform cabinet 2.0 m tall and 0.60 m wide weighs 400 N. A horizontal force is applied at its top edge. What is the smallest force that will start to tip it about its bottom edge?
questions.explanation: About the pivot edge, the weight acts 0.30 m away, giving 400 × 0.30 = 120 N m. The push at 2.0 m must match it: F × 2.0 = 120, so F = 60 N. Using the full width of 0.60 m as the lever arm for the weight gives 120 N.

questions.stem: A truck is parked across a steep sideways slope. When will it tip over?
options: When the slope reaches 45°, whatever load the truck is carrying
When the normal forces on its two sides become exactly equal
When the vertical line through its centre of mass falls outside its wheels
When its centre of mass rises higher than the tops of its wheels on the slope
questions.explanation: The truck tips once its weight, acting at the centre of mass, has a line of action outside the downhill wheels, because the weight’s torque about those wheels then turns it over. A high load raises the centre of mass and makes this happen on a gentler slope, so no single angle applies.

questions.stem: Why does a tower crane carry a heavy counterweight on the short arm opposite the load?
options: The counterweight reduces the weight of the load hanging from the jib
The counterweight’s torque about the tower balances the torque from the load
The counterweight raises the crane’s centre of mass, making it more stable
The counterweight increases the tension in the cable that lifts the load
questions.explanation: The load on the long jib produces a large torque about the tower. The counterweight on the opposite side produces an opposing torque, so the net torque on the tower stays small and it remains in rotational equilibrium.

questions.stem: A uniform 3.0 m balcony beam weighing 600 N is fixed into a wall at one end and sticks out horizontally. A 400 N load hangs from its free end. What torque must the wall supply?
questions.explanation: The beam’s weight acts at its centre, 1.5 m out: 600 × 1.5 = 900 N m. The load gives 400 × 3.0 = 1200 N m. The wall must balance the total of 2100 N m. Putting both weights at the free end gives 3000 N m.

questions.stem: A uniform 10 m bridge span weighing 2.0 × 10⁴ N rests on supports at its two ends. A truck weighing 1.0 × 10⁴ N stands 2.0 m from the left end. What upward force does the left support exert?
questions.explanation: Taking torques about the right support: F × 10 = 2.0 × 10⁴ × 5.0 + 1.0 × 10⁴ × 8.0 = 1.8 × 10⁵ N m, so F = 1.8 × 10⁴ N. The truck is nearer the left end, so the left support carries more. 1.2 × 10⁴ N is the right support’s share.

questions.stem: A uniform 4.0 m beam weighing 800 N is hinged to a wall and held horizontal by a cable from its far end, which makes an angle of 30° with the beam. What is the tension in the cable?
questions.explanation: About the hinge, the weight gives 800 × 2.0 = 1600 N m. Only the cable’s component at right angles to the beam, T sin 30°, gives a torque: T × 0.50 × 4.0 = 1600, so T = 800 N. Ignoring the angle gives 400 N, and using cos 30° gives 460 N.

questions.stem: What is stress?
options: Force multiplied by extension, measured in joules
Force per unit cross-sectional area, measured in pascals
Extension per unit original length, which has no unit
Stress divided by strain, measured in pascals
questions.explanation: Stress is σ = F/A, so its unit is N m⁻², or pascals. Extension divided by original length is strain, and stress divided by strain is Young’s modulus.

questions.stem: A steel rod with a cross-sectional area of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² carries a tensile load of 5.0 × 10⁴ N. What is the stress in the rod?
options: 10 Pa
questions.explanation: σ = F/A = 5.0 × 10⁴ ÷ 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.5 × 10⁸ Pa. Multiplying force by area gives 10, and dividing area by force gives 4.0 × 10⁻⁹. Dividing by a very small area gives a very large stress.

questions.stem: A wire 2.0 m long stretches by 1.0 mm under a load. What is the strain?
questions.explanation: ε = Δl/l = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m ÷ 2.0 m = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴. Dividing the length by the extension gives 2.0 × 10³, and 0.50 comes from not converting millimetres to metres.

questions.stem: Why does strain have no unit?
options: It is a percentage, and percentages are counted as having units
It is a ratio of two lengths: extension divided by original length
It is a ratio of two forces: the load divided by the breaking force
It is measured in pascals, which have been cancelled by the area
questions.explanation: Strain is Δl/l, a length divided by a length, so the units cancel. It is sometimes quoted as a percentage, but it remains a pure ratio. Pascals are the unit of stress and of Young’s modulus.

questions.stem: A sample under a stress of 6.0 × 10⁷ Pa has a strain of 2.0 × 10⁻³ and is behaving elastically. What is its Young’s modulus?
options: 3.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa
questions.explanation: E = σ/ε = 6.0 × 10⁷ ÷ 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 3.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa. Multiplying gives 1.2 × 10⁵, and 3.0 × 10⁴ comes from subtracting the powers of ten wrongly: dividing by 10⁻³ adds 3 to the power.

questions.stem: A steel rod 3.0 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² carries a tension of 2.0 × 10⁴ N. Steel’s Young’s modulus is 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. By how much does the rod stretch?
options: 3.0 mm
1.0 mm
30 mm
questions.explanation: The stress is 2.0 × 10⁴ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁸ Pa, so the strain is 2.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 2.0 × 10¹¹ = 1.0 × 10⁻³. The extension is ε × l = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × 3.0 = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m. Stopping at the strain and reading it as 1.0 mm forgets the length.

questions.stem: What is the unit of Young’s modulus?
options: The newton metre
The joule
The pascal
It has no unit
questions.explanation: Young’s modulus is stress ÷ strain. Stress is in pascals and strain has no unit, so Young’s modulus is in pascals, often quoted in GPa. It is strain, not Young’s modulus, that has no unit.

questions.stem: Material A has a larger Young’s modulus than material B. What can be concluded from this alone?
options: A is stiffer: under the same stress, it strains less than B
A is more flexible: under the same stress, it strains more than B
A is stronger: it can take a greater stress before it breaks
A is tougher: it absorbs more energy per unit volume before breaking
questions.explanation: Young’s modulus measures stiffness, the stress needed per unit of strain, so a larger modulus means less strain for the same stress. Strength and toughness are separate properties: glass is stiffer than many plastics but far less tough.

questions.stem: What is plastic deformation?
options: A change of shape that remains after the load is removed
A change of shape that disappears once the load is removed
A change of shape that happens in plastics but never in metals
A change of shape that only happens when a body is compressed
questions.explanation: Beyond the elastic limit, a material deforms permanently: when the load is removed it does not return to its original shape. Elastic deformation disappears when the load is removed. Metals such as copper can deform plastically a great deal.

questions.stem: A wire is loaded beyond its elastic limit and then unloaded. What happens?
options: It becomes shorter than it was before it was loaded
It snaps at the moment the load is taken off it
It does not return to its original length; it stays stretched
It returns exactly to its original length once unloaded
questions.explanation: Past the elastic limit, part of the deformation is plastic and permanent, so the wire stays longer than it was. Below the elastic limit it would return exactly to its original length.

questions.stem: On a stress–strain graph, what does the straight section starting at the origin show?
options: Plastic behaviour, with stress proportional to strain; its gradient is the toughness
Elastic behaviour, with stress proportional to strain; its gradient is Young’s modulus
Plastic behaviour, with permanent stretching; its gradient is the breaking stress
Elastic behaviour, with stress proportional to strain; its area is Young’s modulus
questions.explanation: In the straight, elastic section, stress is proportional to strain and the material returns to its shape when unloaded. The gradient, σ/ε, is Young’s modulus. The area under the graph is energy per unit volume, not the modulus.

questions.stem: What does the area under a stress–strain graph up to the breaking point represent?
options: The ultimate tensile strength, the highest stress the material reaches
The energy absorbed per unit volume before fracture, which measures toughness
The Young’s modulus of the material, which is a measure of its stiffness
The total force that the sample of material can carry before it breaks
questions.explanation: Stress × strain has units of N m⁻² × (m/m) = J m⁻³, so the area is energy absorbed per cubic metre. A material that absorbs a lot of energy before breaking is tough. The ultimate tensile strength is the peak height of the graph, not its area.

questions.stem: In its elastic region, a sample reaches a strain of 0.0020 at a stress of 4.0 × 10⁸ Pa. How much energy per cubic metre is stored in it?
options: 2.0 × 10¹¹ J m⁻³
questions.explanation: The elastic section is a straight line from the origin, so the area is a triangle: ½ × 4.0 × 10⁸ × 0.0020 = 4.0 × 10⁵ J m⁻³. Leaving out the ½ gives 8.0 × 10⁵, and 2.0 × 10¹¹ is σ/ε, the Young’s modulus.

questions.stem: A material’s stress–strain graph is a straight line all the way to the point where it breaks. How is this material described?
options: Infinitely stiff, as its strain never changes with stress
Brittle, like glass, with little or no plastic region
Ductile, like copper, as it stretches far before breaking
Plastic throughout, so it never returns to its shape
questions.explanation: A brittle material deforms elastically and then fractures suddenly, with almost no plastic deformation, so its graph stays straight to the end. A ductile material has a long curved plastic region before it breaks.

questions.stem: On a stress–strain graph, material X has a steep straight line that ends suddenly at a small strain. Material Y has a gentler slope, then a long plastic region, and a much larger area under its graph. Which comparison is correct?
options: Y is stiffer and brittle; X is less stiff and tougher
X and Y are equally tough, as both of them break
X is stiffer but brittle; Y is less stiff but tougher
X is less stiff but tougher; Y is stiffer but brittle
questions.explanation: The steeper initial gradient means X has the larger Young’s modulus and is stiffer, but breaking with no plastic region makes it brittle. Y’s larger area means it absorbs more energy before breaking, so it is tougher.

questions.stem: A concrete has a compressive strength of 40 MPa and a tensile strength of 4 MPa. For which use is plain, unreinforced concrete best suited?
options: A tie rod holding two walls together
A long beam spanning a wide gap unsupported
A column carrying the weight of a building
A cable holding up a section of bridge deck
questions.explanation: Concrete is ten times stronger in compression than in tension here, so it suits members that are squashed, like columns. Cables and tie rods are in tension, and a long beam has a tensile lower surface, so plain concrete would crack in all three.

questions.stem: Why are steel cables, rather than concrete, used to hang the deck of a suspension bridge?
options: Steel has a low Young’s modulus, so it stretches to absorb the load
Concrete is stronger in tension, but it is too heavy to lift into place
Steel is brittle, so the cables will not stretch under the deck’s load
Steel has a high tensile strength, while concrete is weak in tension
questions.explanation: The hanging cables are in tension, so the material must have a high tensile strength, which steel does. Concrete cracks under quite small tensile stresses. Steel is stiff, with a high Young’s modulus, and it is ductile rather than brittle.

questions.stem: Materials P and Q have the same tensile strength. P has a Young’s modulus of 200 GPa and Q has 70 GPa. A designer needs a tie that stretches as little as possible under a given load. Which should be chosen, and why?
options: Q, because its lower Young’s modulus gives less strain for the same stress
Either, because equal tensile strengths mean they stretch by equal amounts
Q, because a lower Young’s modulus always means a higher breaking stress
P, because its higher Young’s modulus gives less strain for the same stress
questions.explanation: For the same stress, strain = σ/E, so the material with the larger E strains less. P strains only about a third as much as Q. Tensile strength describes when a material breaks, not how much it stretches before then.

questions.stem: A fishing rod must bend a long way under load and spring back without damage. Which combination of properties suits it best?
options: A large plastic region, so that it stays bent after use
A fairly low Young’s modulus and a large elastic range
A very high Young’s modulus and a small elastic range
A high compressive strength and brittle behaviour
questions.explanation: A lower Young’s modulus lets the rod strain a lot under a modest stress, so it is flexible, and a large elastic range means it returns to shape. A material that deforms plastically would stay bent, and a brittle one would snap.

questions.stem: Why are ceramics used for parts such as tiles and engine coatings that are not loaded in tension?
options: Ceramics are strong in compression but brittle, failing suddenly in tension
Ceramics are ductile, so they stretch a long way before breaking in tension
Ceramics have a very low Young’s modulus, so they bend easily under load
Ceramics are much weaker in compression than they are in tension
questions.explanation: Ceramics are hard, stiff and strong in compression and withstand high temperatures, but they are brittle, so a crack under tension spreads suddenly. Designers therefore keep them in compression. They are neither ductile nor flexible.

questions.stem: Carbon-fibre composites are used in some modern structures. What makes them effective?
options: Strong, stiff fibres carry the tensile load, while a matrix binds them and spreads the load
Two brittle materials are combined so the composite is even more brittle than either one
A metal and a plastic are melted together to form a single, uniform alloy of the two
The fibres carry compression only, while the matrix around them carries all of the tension
questions.explanation: In a fibre composite, fibres with very high tensile strength and stiffness are embedded in a resin matrix that holds them in place and transfers the load between them. The combination is strong, stiff and light. It is not an alloy, and the matrix is much weaker in tension than the fibres.

questions.stem: A steel cable of cross-sectional area 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² carries a load of 1.0 × 10⁵ N. Its breaking stress is 4.0 × 10⁸ Pa. What is the stress in the cable, and how does it compare with the breaking stress?
options: 50 Pa, far below the breaking stress
5.0 × 10⁸ Pa, above the breaking stress
2.0 × 10⁸ Pa, half the breaking stress
2.0 × 10⁸ Pa, twice the breaking stress
questions.explanation: σ = F/A = 1.0 × 10⁵ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁸ Pa, which is half of 4.0 × 10⁸ Pa, so the cable is safe with a margin. Multiplying force by area gives 50.

questions.stem: A concrete column with a cross-sectional area of 0.20 m² carries a compressive load of 1.0 × 10⁶ N. The concrete’s compressive strength is 4.0 × 10⁷ Pa. What is the compressive stress, and is the column safe?
options: 5.0 × 10⁶ Pa, well within the compressive strength
2.0 × 10⁵ Pa, well within the compressive strength
5.0 × 10⁶ Pa, above the compressive strength
2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, half the compressive strength
questions.explanation: σ = F/A = 1.0 × 10⁶ ÷ 0.20 = 5.0 × 10⁶ Pa, an eighth of the 4.0 × 10⁷ Pa the concrete can withstand. 2.0 × 10⁵ comes from multiplying the load by the area.

questions.stem: A news report claims a new material is ‘ten times stronger than steel’. Which question best tests the physics of this claim?
options: How many people have shared the news report online since it was first published?
Does the new material look and feel much the same as steel does when you handle it?
Which property is meant, such as tensile strength or stiffness, and is there published test data?
Is the company that makes the material a well-known brand that people already trust?
questions.explanation: ‘Strong’ can mean tensile strength, compressive strength, stiffness or toughness, and these differ greatly. A valid claim names the property and is supported by repeatable, published test data. Brand, popularity and appearance say nothing about the physics.

questions.stem: Engineers model a steel beam using Young’s modulus, E = σ/ε. What is a limitation of this model?
options: It applies only to materials loaded in compression, never in tension
It applies only to plastics and rubbers, because metals have no Young’s modulus
It applies only after the material has begun to deform plastically
It applies only in the elastic region, where stress is proportional to strain
questions.explanation: Young’s modulus describes the straight, elastic part of a stress–strain graph. Beyond the limit of proportionality the graph curves, so a single value of E no longer predicts the strain. Young’s modulus applies in both tension and compression.
